scenes.tts: Shine blue light on cells in a mouse's dentate gyrus, and the mouse freezes. Those cells were tagged while it learned to fear one box. But now the mouse is in a different box. Headlines said scientists had found where the memory is stored. Had it?
scenes.visual: Box A with the dentate cells active during learning, then a different box B; blue light on the tagged cells and the mouse state flips to FREEZING; then a large question mark: was the memory found?
scenes.narration: Shine blue light on cells in a mouse's dentate gyrus, and the mouse freezes. Those cells were tagged while it learned to fear one box. But now the mouse is in a different box. Headlines said scientists had found where the memory is stored. Had it?

scenes.tts: How are the cells tagged? C fos is a gene switched on in recently active neurons. The group used its promoter to put an opsin, channelrhodopsin two, into dentate gyrus cells active during learning. Mice were off a drug, doxycycline, for one or two days before training, and back on it afterwards. That restricted the tagging. Light now switches on just those cells.

scenes.visual: Large dentate gyrus box of cells; the learning-active ones turn yellow and show c-fos on; blue opsin rings mark them while the others stay unringed; a doxycycline window bar; blue light lights only the ringed cells.

scenes.tts: Days later, light on those cells made the mice freeze in a different context. Two controls made this specific. Cells tagged in a neutral context did not evoke fear freezing. Mice with a fluorescent protein but no opsin did not freeze to light. The pulses were twenty hertz, which describes the intervention, not how the cells fire in natural recall. So activating the tagged cells is enough to produce the behaviour. That is sufficiency, in this preparation.

scenes.visual: Three rows: fear-tagged cells plus light give FREEZING; neutral-context tag plus light gives no freezing; fluorescent protein only plus light gives no freezing; a 20 Hz note labelled as the tool, not the natural firing; then the word sufficiency.

scenes.tts: Enough is not the same as needed. The authors themselves noted this. Necessity needs silencing during natural recall. Kitamura and colleagues tagged prefrontal cells in mice at learning, then inhibited them later. Natural cue recall failed on day twelve. It did not fail on day two. So the cells were needed at the later delay, not the earlier one.

scenes.visual: Header contrasts light-on (sufficient) with silence-during-natural-recall (necessity). Two panels, day 2 and day 12, each with prefrontal tagged cells that are silenced; day 2 recall stays intact, day 12 recall fails.

scenes.tts: So where is the memory? Roy and colleagues mapped learning-activated cells across two hundred forty seven mouse brain regions. They flagged one hundred seventeen as likely engram candidates. Reactivating several ensembles together gave more recall than reactivating one. Where the memory is may have more than one answer.

scenes.visual: A grid of 247 squares, one per region (not a map); 117 turn orange as likely engram candidates; then one ensemble versus several together with more recall.

scenes.tts: Keep the rule. Light that triggers freezing shows sufficiency. Necessity needs silencing during natural recall. All of this is mouse fear learning over days, not human memory over years. Sufficiency is not necessity. Ask which control each claim needs.
scenes.visual: Two columns: light drives cells gives freezing (sufficient) and silence during natural recall gives failed recall (needed); a not-equal sign; a bounds chip mouse contextual fear over days; the rule line.
